articles.title: I Am Artemis: Allison Mjoen
paras: As the supercooled propellant flowed into the core stage, and NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket roared to life, Allison Mjoen and her family watched with awe and pride.
Mjoen, NASA’s operations manager for the agency’s Exploration Ground Systems Program, helped shape the systems and ground operations that will one day send humans back to the Moon.

Over her 20-year career at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, she supported missions across the Space Shuttle Program, the International Space Station, and now she is applying that experience to Artemis.
April 1, 2026, was a bright, crystal-clear day along the Florida Space Coast.
The sunlight seemed to sharpen every color along the horizon.
As Mjoen and her children counted down and the crowd’s voices rose around them, the rumble of the SLS rocket intensified beneath their feet.
For her children, it was the chance to see what their mom had helped make possible.
For Mjoen, it was a moment she would never forget.
That moment also offered a pause for reflection on the work that led her there.
As the spacecraft offline operations manager, Mjoen coordinates the work that happens long before launch day.

By supporting the ground systems’ senior vehicle operations manager, Matt Czech , she develops integration plans and oversees ground operations for Artemis vehicle processing, focusing on booster and Orion spacecraft operations.
Mjoen began her career as a flight crew systems engineer with United Space Alliance supporting the Space Shuttle Program.
Her team handled mission-specific cabin configurations, including the food, spacesuits, cargo, and payloads astronauts needed aboard the shuttle.
After the Space Shuttle Program retired, she supported the International Space Station Program as a payload integration engineer.
In this role, she connected experiment investigators with the organizations developing their hardware.

She later worked in the Project Office on the Test and Operations Support Contract before joining NASA’s Operations Project Engineering Office, where she served as the Spacecraft Payloads Integration and Evolution Element lead for Artemis I.
“Early on, I thought every decision had to be perfect, but everything is an opportunity to learn, especially the tasks that seem unrelated at the time.
It’s about staying curious, working hard, building relationships, and trusting that each step is preparing you for the next one.
Allison Mjoen
That preparation took on new meaning when she first supported integrated firing room operations as a certified operations project engineer during Artemis I.
Earning the certification was a milestone.
Applying it during real time operations brought a new level of responsibility.
“Every decision and communication directly supported the integrated team’s ability to execute safely and properly implement the test procedure,” said Mjoen.
Working at the integration console underscored the importance of preparation, collaboration and trust — lessons she carries into her work coordinating across teams today.
“I get to collaborate everyday with incredibly talented and dedicated people who are all working toward the same goal.
It’s especially rewarding to know that our collective efforts directly contribute to the success of the mission.”
Allison Mjoen
For Mjoen, the shared experience is part of what makes Artemis so important.
As the Artemis program continues, she looks forward to another moment families will be able to share as astronauts return to the lunar surface.
“That single moment captured the imagination of people around the world and showed what is possible when we come together for a bold goal,” she said of the first Apollo Moon landing.
“Artemis is creating that kind of moment for a whole new generation, and this time to stay.”

articles.title: NASA Satellites Observe Historic 2026 El Niño
paras: A phenomenon rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system is unfolding this fall, and NASA is tracking it closely.
El Niño is a natural climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific.
NASA scientists are keeping watch as it flips trade winds, redistributes ocean heat, scrambles rain patterns, and raises sea surface height across parts of the Pacific.
As of October, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has said that there’s an 83% chance that the strongest El Niño since 1950 is currently unfolding.
People around the world, including farmers, firefighters, and coastal communities, are already experiencing the effects in different ways.
Follow along with these maps as NASA tracks El Niño from its epicenter in the equatorial Pacific Ocean.
One of the first clues appeared in satellite imagery in January 2026, when a swell of warm water called a Kelvin wave was spotted near Micronesia in the western Pacific.
Kelvin waves are slow-moving pulses of water thousands of miles long.
Like underwater freeways, they transfer heat from west to east across the Pacific.
The warm water heats the air directly above it, making it rise.

The change in air pressures weakens or even reverses the trade winds that typically blow in the opposing direction, from the Americas toward Asia, causing sea levels in the eastern Pacific to rise further, and waters to warm even more.
This chain reaction signifies the start of an El Niño.
The map above shows that by early April, those Kelvin waves had reached the eastern Pacific, and sea surface temperatures had begun to warm.
Warm water expands in volume, elevating local sea levels in some areas by as much as 1 to 1.3 feet (30 to 40 centimeters).
The higher-than-normal water can be seen sloshing toward South America then moving up the coast to California.
Sea levels that are six to eight inches (15 to 20 centimeters) lower than normal are visible around Indonesia and northern Australia.
“Kelvin waves are like the heartbeat of El Niño,” said Josh Willis, project scientist for sea level missions at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.
“And our sea level satellites let us peer into the ocean and watch every beat.”
Scientists have used satellite altimetry to track the height of the ocean with ultraprecision since 1993.
That unbroken data record continues today with the Sentinel-6 satellites .

State-of-the-art radar altimeters aboard these satellites survey millions of square miles of ocean in a single day, complementing NOAA’s fleet of ocean sensors and buoys drifting and diving through the water below.
Warmer-than-normal seawater is one of the best-known indicators of El Niño.

Already, sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific are about 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.7 degrees Celsius) warmer than the long-term average and could jump another fraction of a degree in the coming months, Willis said.
Satellites carrying microwave and infrared radiometers can see through and around clouds to measure heat energy at the sea surface.
Satellites in 2026 mapped the band of warmer-than-normal water as it expanded throughout the spring.
The band, seen in dark red, stretches for millions of square miles from the heart of the Pacific to the coast of South America.
Ocean temperatures can influence weather patterns around the world.
Air above the water’s surface carries heat and moisture into the atmosphere, seeding rainstorms and rearranging weather patterns across the globe.
El Niño’s warm waters also change the color of the ocean.
A NASA satellite is tracking these subtle shifts in hues, as equatorial Pacific waters have become measurably more blue over the last several months.

“Some people think of water as being just blue, but it’s amazing the multitude of colors the ocean can be,” said Matthew Kehrli, a lead research scientist for the PACE (Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem) satellite team at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.
This spectrum is in part thanks to microscopic plants called phytoplankton, which form the basis of the marine food web.
There are thousands of different species of phytoplankton, which come in shades like teal, brown, or green.
This year, in areas of the Pacific Ocean along the equator that are typically lush with phytoplankton and greener as a result, these hues are waning.
This is an expected effect of El Niño.
Phytoplankton thrive in cool, nutrient-rich waters, but during an El Niño, the weakening trade winds reduce the upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface.
With limited food supply, phytoplankton abundance drops.
This decline can trigger cascading effects across the marine food web, forcing other marine life to relocate to new feeding grounds.
This year’s El Niño is the first since PACE launched in 2024, providing new views of the phenomenon.

The Ocean Color Instrument aboard PACE observes the ocean in hyperspectral color — across several hundred different wavelengths of visible, near-infrared, and ultraviolet light — monitoring phytoplankton and other ocean-color changes in near-real time.
With PACE data, researchers calculate the average color of the ocean, simplifying spectra of light into a single number, known as apparent visible wavelength.
The 2026 map above shows the green area along the equator in the western Pacific Ocean shrink as a bluer shade fills in, indicating fewer phytoplankton.
In contrast, the map from 2025 shows how the green-hued section stays steady over time.
“You have expectations of what you would think would happen,” Kehrli said.
“But to visually see the results with the data products that you’re working with in real time is gratifying.”
NASA scientists will continue to monitor the signs and impacts of this El Niño with its fleet of Earth-observing satellites.
“El Niño touches almost all of us in some way every time it occurs,” Willis said.
“While many have seen what it can do, we look to the ocean to understand why.”

articles.title: Power Up: Roll Out Solar Arrays Boost Space Station Power Supply
paras: From the International Space Station’s unique position 250 miles above Earth, the Sun is a vital source of energy.
Solar power supports the station’s life support systems, daily activities, and hundreds of research investigations that improve life on Earth and prepare humans for deep space exploration.
Over the past five years, NASA augmented the station’s power generation and distribution capability with next-generation International Space Station Roll Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs).
In 2017, a technology demonstration conducted aboard the space station tested the effectiveness of the arrays .
The lightweight, compact design launches as a cylinder and unfurls like a yoga mat after installation.
This advanced design reduces mass and volume at launch and uses an autonomous, self-deploying system that minimizes risks during rollout.
The IROSAs were designed, manufactured, and tested by Redwire under a contract with Boeing and are about half the size of the station’s legacy arrays.
Despite being smaller, the arrays are capable of producing about 28 kilowatts of additional power.
Six IROSAs were installed outside of the space station between 2021 and 2023.

In 2023, power projections prompted a request for another set of IROSAs, which launched in Dragon spacecraft’s trunk during the SpaceX 35th commercial resupply services mission to space station for NASA.
Together, the eight IROSAs will increase power by more than 160kW for research and operations.

With the full upgrade in place, the space station’s revitalized power system not only supports NASA’s legacy in low Earth orbit but also helps advance technology that will extend the agency’s reach into the solar system.

From planetary defense demonstrations, like the Double Asteroid Redirection Test , to future human exploration efforts, the space station is an essential testbed for the technologies needed for expeditions beyond Earth’s orbit.

articles.title: NASA to Help Unlock Mysteries of Mars’ Moons in Upcoming Mission
paras: NASA is playing an important role in JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of Mars’ moons and build on the agency’s long history of exploring the Red Planet.
The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of Mars’ moons Phobos and Deimos and deliver a sample of Phobos to Earth.
The MMX spacecraft is targeting launch from JAXA’s Tanegashima Space Center in Japan at 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. JST on Tuesday, Oct. 20).

“The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington.

“The NASA-JAXA sample curation partnership is extremely valuable, and I am proud that NASA Science is supporting MMX sample curation and will be sharing portions of these samples for study as we continue to expand humanity’s understanding of the universe for the benefit of all.”

NASA’s contributions to the mission include the Mars-moon Exploration with Gamma rays and Neutrons (MEGANE) spectrograph instrument, the Pneumatic Sampler (P-Sampler) technology demonstration, and communications and navigation support from the agency’s Deep Space Network , as well as funding United States scientists participating on the MMX science team.
Scientists have long debated the origin of Mars’ two moons.
The data and samples collected by the MMX mission will help answer essential questions about the origins of these moons and the history of the solar system.

“Phobos and Deimos may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars’ gravity billions of years ago,” said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters.
“Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds.”

The MEGANE (pronounced meh-GAH-nay, the Japanese word for eyeglasses) spectrograph will help scientists “see” what Phobos is made of by measuring neutrons and gamma rays emitted from the moon’s surface and determining its chemical elemental composition, which will provide important clues about its origin.
Mounted on one of the spacecraft’s landing legs, the P-Sampler is designed to collect a ground sample from Phobos.
The system gathers surface material using bursts of high-pressure nitrogen gas, complementing JAXA’s C-Sampler, which will extract cores from a few inches deeper.
NASA will obtain and curate about 15% of the total returned sample at the agency’s Johnson Space Center Astromaterials Lab in Houston, making it available for research for decades.
Another key part of NASA’s contribution to MMX is its scientific partnership with JAXA.

NASA-supported researchers are working alongside international colleagues to help reveal the story of Phobos and will use mission data and returned samples to uncover new clues about the moon’s origin and the evolution of the Mars system.
The MMX spacecraft will arrive at Mars in August 2027 to begin its survey of the Red Planet’s two moons.
After surveying Phobos in detail, the spacecraft will collect a sample of the moon’s surface no earlier than December 2028 and deliver it to Earth in 2031.
The MEGANE instrument was developed by the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.
Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, developed the spacecraft’s pneumatic sampler mechanism.
NASA’s contributions to the MMX mission were developed under the agency’s Discovery Program.
The Discovery Program is managed by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, for the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington.

articles.title: NASA’s Chandra Breaks Down ‘Treble Clef’s’ Galaxy Cluster Collision
paras: Astronomers have used NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the “Treble Clef” because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol.
The researchers discovered the Treble Clef is likely caused by an outburst from a supermassive black hole, followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters.
A paper describing the findings, led by Andrea Botteon of the National Institute for Astrophysics, or INAF, in Italy, published Wednesday in the Astronomy & Astrophysics journal .

An explanation for the Treble Clef has been particularly difficult to find because the formation lies almost directly behind the plane of the Milky Way, meaning that stars, gas, and dust from our home galaxy largely block the view from Earth.
However, by using telescopes that can peer through the intervening material, a team of researchers was able to identify what is responsible for this uncommon structure.

NASA’s Chandra and the German Extended RÖntgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) X-ray telescope found diffuse, hot gas at the location of the Treble Clef, showing that a galaxy cluster hosts the object.
The researchers also determined the galaxy cluster is, in fact, two clusters in the process of merging.
Galaxy clusters are some of the largest structures in the universe, containing hundreds of individual galaxies and huge reservoirs of superheated gas.

This new composite image of the Treble Clef and its cluster shows the multimillion-degree gas detected in X-rays by Chandra and eROSITA in blue, with some of the Chandra data derived from a special technique the authors used to highlight important features in the Chandra data.
Radio data shown in red from the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR), a large network of radio telescopes in Europe reveals the doppelganger of the musical notation.
The final piece of the combined image comes from infrared data obtained by the United Kingdom Infrared Telescope, appearing mostly white.
The authors concluded that the Treble Clef likely formed in a two-stage process.
First, an earlier outburst from a supermassive black hole in the galaxy cluster’s center drove clouds of charged particles and magnetic fields away at close to the speed of light.
This led to a type of cosmic crescendo and initially produced bright radio waves that later faded as the particles lost energy.
Next, the collision between the two clusters compressed or reenergized the cloud, which became brighter again in radio waves.
Shock waves — similar to the sonic booms from supersonic jets — from the collision may have played a role in this reenergizing process.
To reveal evidence for the cluster collision in the Chandra data, the authors used a special technique that examined how much the cluster’s hot gas deviates from a symmetrical shape.
Most of the hot gas is symmetrical and shaped approximately like an oval.
The authors removed this symmetrical oval shape from the original X-ray image.
The remaining X-ray emission in the residual image shows t is brightest on the left and right, and faintest in the center.
The new composite image combines both the original X-ray and the residual X-ray images.

The brighter X-rays in the residual image, toward the left and right of the cluster’s center, imply that the collision between the two clusters likely occurred along the left-right direction as seen in the image.
The researchers think the direct collision between the two clusters occurred a few hundred million years ago, and the clusters are now moving away from each other.
The resemblance to a treble clef is a case of pareidolia, the phenomenon when people see familiar shapes in random data, since there is no scientific connection to the musical notation.
NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, manages the Chandra program.
The Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory’s Chandra X-ray Center controls science operations from Cambridge, Massachusetts, and flight operations from Burlington, Massachusetts.
This release features a composite image of a remarkable radio wave formation that strongly resembles a treble clef musical symbol, hovering in the midst of two colliding galaxy clusters.
Here, galaxies in the galaxy clusters, plus foreground and background stars and galaxies, blanket the image with specks of light set against the blackness of space.
At the center of the frame is a large, oval, blue-purple cloud with ragged edges.
This is a multimillion-degree gas cloud in the two clusters detected in X-rays by Chandra and eROSITA, the Extended RÖntgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array.
In the middle of the purple field, tilting slightly to our left, is what appears to be a giant treble clef, loosely drawn with a neon pink marker.
Like the musical notation for which it’s named, the formation has a strong vertical stroke with a continuous, fluid line swooping back and forth as it moves from top to bottom.
This radio wave formation appears to be the result of a two-stage process.
First, charged particles and magnetic fields were driven from a supermassive black hole, producing bright radio waves.
Those waves faded and lost energy over time, before being reenergized and compressed when the two galaxy clusters collided.

articles.title: Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 Completes Environmental Testing at NASA JPL
paras: A lunar lander from Voyager Technologies completed nearly three months of environmental testing at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California in late September 2026.
The tests demonstrate that the spacecraft is prepared to face the harsh conditions of launch, its journey to the Moon, and landing on the surface.

Its final trial was in JPL’s historic 25-Foot Space Simulator, a thermal vacuum chamber listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its role in supporting historic missions like those of the Ranger, Surveyor, Mariner, and Voyager programs.

Engineers and technicians on Aug. 31, 2026, used a crane to position the spacecraft within the towering chamber, where Griffin-1 alternately baked at up to 167 degrees Fahrenheit (75 degrees Celsius) and froze at temperatures as low as minus 148 F (minus 100 C).
This thermal vacuum testing simulates the extreme temperatures the spacecraft will experience during its mission.
The yellow-striped box atop the lander simulates a payload that will later be attached to the spacecraft: Astrolab’s FLIP (FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform) rover.
In Figure A, engineers and technicians move Griffin-1 through a hallway leading to the 25-Foot Space Simulator on Aug. 31.
The corridor is lined with photographs of some of the historic spacecraft that have been tested in the facility since the 1960s.

Figure B shows Griffin-1 on July 29 in an anechoic chamber for electromagnetic interference and electromagnetic compatibility testing, which ensures signals from the spacecraft’s electronic components don’t interfere with one another.
Long foam spikes line the chamber walls to absorb sound waves and electromagnetic waves.

In Figure C, taken on July 20, Griffin-1 rotates rapidly on a special table to measure its mass properties, enabling engineers to look for any unexpected wobbles as they assess how the vehicle will move through space — vital information for determining the spacecraft’s readiness for flight and surface operations.

In Figure D, microphones are arrayed around Griffin-1 on Aug. 12 during acoustic testing in which giant horns powered by compressed gaseous nitrogen blast the spacecraft with up to 153 decibels inside the sealed acoustic chamber to mimic the roar of launch.

Griffin-1 also endured vibration testing, during which hundreds of sensors monitored the spacecraft as a “shaker table” rattled it in three directions — with increasingly intense force — to simulate the ride out of Earth’s atmosphere atop a rocket.
After proving its mettle at JPL, Griffin-1 was shipped back across the country to Voyager Lunar Systems’ Pittsburgh facility for final assembly.
Part of NASA’s CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative within the Moon Base Program, Griffin-1 is expected to launch in late 2026 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.
The infrastructure-class lander will deliver more than 1,100 pounds (455 kilograms) of cargo — 10 payloads from six countries — to Nobile Crater near the lunar South Pole.
Caltech in Pasadena, California, manages JPL for NASA.

articles.title: TB 26-08 Complex Modes in Lightly Damped Structural Systems: A Two-Mode Interaction Perspective
paras: For more information, contact Joel W.
Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov
Complex mode shapes can emerge in a linear structure even when overall damping is low.
This behavior can occur when two structural modes are closely spaced in frequency and are coupled through nonproportional damping.
As the damping interaction increases, the two modal frequencies move toward one another while the mode shapes become increasingly complex.
At a critical interaction level, the two frequencies coalesce.
Beyond this point, the frequencies remain approximately equal while the modal decay rates separate.
At very strong interaction, the mode shapes become approximately real again, but as different combinations of the original uncoupled modes.
This framework provides a simple physical interpretation of mode veering, complex mode formation, eigenvalue coalescence, and decay-rate splitting in lightly damped structural systems.
Why Complex Modes Can Appear at Low Damping Classical modal analysis often treats lightly damped structures as nearly proportional systems with real mode shapes.
That interpretation can become misleading when two modes are closely spaced.
In modal coordinates, nonproportional damping introduces an off-diagonal coupling term ε.
The relevant question is therefore not simply whether damping is small, but whether the coupling is large relative to the baseline half-frequency separation δ=(ω2 -ω1 )/2.
Reduced Perturbation Framework For a closely spaced pair, define the central eigenvalue λ0 ≈-ζω +iω and write the coupled eigenvalues as λ1,2=λ0 ±s.
Under lightdamping and close-mode asymptotic assumptions, the local quartic eigenvalue problem reduces to s²=ε²/4-δ².
This single relation determines the direction of eigenvalue separation in the complex plane, as summarized in Figure. 1.
For 0<ε 2δ, s = ±β and the split is predominantly horizontal (decay rate).
As ε increases further, β increases and the two decay rates separate more strongly while their frequencies remain approximately equal.
Engineering Interpretation and Recommended Practice Complexity in an identified mode shape should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of heavy damping, nonlinearity, or poor test data.
For a close modal pair, examine the complex poles together with mode-shape phase.

Frequency convergence accompanied by near-quadrature modal components is consistent with the imaginary-s regime; nearly equal frequencies accompanied by decay-rate separation is consistent with the real-s regime.
The framework also provides a practical testanalysis bridge: s=(λ1 -λ2 )/2 can be obtained from identified poles, while δ can be estimated from the uncoupled or pretest analytical modal spacing.
These quantities can then be used to estimate the effective interaction strength and determine proximity to the transition boundary.
1. Majed, A., Henkel, E.
E., and Sills, J.
W., Emergence of Complex Modes in Lightly Damped Structural Systems: A Reduced Perturbation Framework, NASA/TM-20260007553, August 2026.

articles.title: NASA Names Astronaut Christina Koch Acting Deputy Chief Engineer
paras: NASA engineer and astronaut Christina Koch will serve as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer beginning on Sunday, Nov. 1, following the retirement of Katherine Van Hooser, who will conclude more than 35 years of distinguished service to the agency on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA’s engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency’s programs and projects.
With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments.
“Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

“After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the Moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role.

I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars.”

“Katherine has been an extraordinary leader throughout her career, bringing technical expertise, sound judgment, and an unwavering commitment to mission success to some of NASA’s most complex engineering challenges,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer.
“Her leadership has strengthened our engineering community and helped guide the agency through critical milestones and transitions.
Christina brings a unique combination of engineering expertise, operational experience, and proven leadership, both on the ground and in space.
I am grateful to Katherine for her exceptional service and confident Christina will continue the tradition of technical excellence that is essential to everything we do at NASA.”
Koch most recently served as a mission specialist aboard NASA’s Artemis II mission in April, helping carry out the first crewed flight around the Moon in more than 50 years.

She previously spent 328 consecutive days aboard the International Space Station, setting the record for the longest single spaceflight by a woman and participating in the first all-female spacewalks.
Koch began her NASA career as an electrical engineer at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, developing scientific instruments for space missions.
Before her selection as an astronaut in 2013, her experience also included scientific field engineering in Antarctica and the Arctic.

She has since held leadership positions within NASA’s Astronaut Office and at the agency’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, bringing a combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and firsthand understanding of the demands of human spaceflight to her new role.
Van Hooser joined NASA in 1991 at the agency’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, beginning a distinguished career in propulsion engineering and technical leadership.
Her early work focused on liquid rocket engine turbomachinery before she became chief engineer for the space shuttle main engine, leading engineering efforts through the final 21 shuttle flights.
She later served as the first chief engineer for the Space Launch System’s Liquid Engines Element, helping advance the propulsion systems supporting NASA’s Artemis missions.
As Marshall’s chief engineer and, since 2023, NASA’s deputy chief engineer, Van Hooser provided critical technical leadership and oversight across the agency’s programs.

Her steady guidance through complex engineering challenges and organizational transitions helped maintain continuity, strengthen collaboration, and keep mission readiness at the forefront of NASA’s work.

articles.title: Antarctic Sea Ice Grows to Its 2026 Maximum
paras: This story is an update to the Antarctic sea ice feature in our World of Change series tracking long-term change on Earth’s surface through satellite imagery.
Unlike the Arctic—an ocean basin surrounded by land—the Antarctic is a large continent surrounded by an ocean.
Because of this geography, sea ice has more room to expand during the winter.
However, that ice also stretches into warmer latitudes, leading to more melting in the summer.
Antarctic sea ice usually peaks in September, around the end of the Southern Hemisphere’s winter, and retreats to a minimum in February.
According to NASA and the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), Antarctic sea ice in 2026 likely reached its annual maximum extent on September 14 (above).
On that date, the ice covered an estimated 17.59 million square kilometers (6.79 million square miles), making it the third-lowest maximum on record.
The maps below show the average concentration of Antarctic sea ice for the month of September (left) and the following February (right) from 1990 to 2026.
Opaque white areas indicate the highest concentrations, and dark blue areas are open water.
The images include only areas where ice concentration was at least 15 percent, a threshold scientists commonly use to count an area as ice-covered in satellite data.
Scientists refer to the total area of these regions as the “sea ice extent.”
From 1979 until 2014, total Antarctic sea ice increased by about 1 percent per decade.
Whether the increase was a sign of meaningful change is uncertain because ice extents vary considerably from year to year around Antarctica.
For three consecutive years, from 2012 to 2014, satellites observed new record highs for winter sea ice extent.
These highs occurred while Arctic ice was in steep decline.
The climb came to an end in 2015, and significant decreases in sea ice around Antarctica started to occur in 2016.
There have since been years with small rebounds, but overall, Antarctic sea ice coverage has largely remained lower than normal.
Both the record low minimum and record low maximum occurred in 2023.
Scientists will continue to observe the area each year to find out if the decline is part of a long-term change or a statistical fluctuation.
To determine sea ice extent, scientists rely on satellites with passive microwave sensors that measure the microwave energy Earth naturally emits.
Sea ice emits more of this energy than open water, so it stands out in microwave images.
Because microwaves pass through clouds, the satellites can observe sea ice regularly, regardless of weather.

The record began in late 1978 with data collected by NASA’s Nimbus-7 , followed by Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites starting in 1987, and by NASA’s Aqua satellite between 2002 and 2011.
In 2025, scientists began using observations from the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s GCOM-W satellite .

articles.title: NASA’s SpaceX CRS-35 Mission to Launch Health Research
paras: NASA experiments focused on human and plant health and drug-resistant organisms will travel to the International Space Station aboard SpaceX’s 35th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, advancing research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration.

This research supports astronaut health during long-duration missions through four investigations from the agency’s Biological and Physical Sciences division, including 3D models of the human brain, a crop disease study, a faster way to assess astronaut health, and an analysis of antibiotic-resistant bacteria aboard the space station.
A new precision health investigation helps address a key question: What happens to the human brain in space?
The experiment sends small, lab-grown models of the human brain to the orbiting laboratory for five weeks.
Researchers compare tissue models that traveled to space with identical ones kept on Earth to determine how a short spaceflight affects the human brain at the cellular level.

The effort could deepen our understanding of how the human brain responds to stress and help lay the groundwork for methods that counter risks to brain health that astronauts may face on future missions to the Moon and beyond.
A space crops investigation tests whether crop diseases develop faster and more severely in microgravity.
The experiment compares molecular and structural changes between Earth-grown and space station-grown plants infected with a disease-causing fungus.
The findings could guide plant breeding on Earth to produce disease-resistant crops and help minimize yield losses in future space agriculture systems.
Space crops provide nutrition, increase dietary variety, and offer psychological benefits for astronauts during extended missions.
They also absorb carbon dioxide, produce oxygen, and recycle water, which will become increasingly important as human missions extend farther from Earth.
The spacecraft also carries the first test of a compact microplate reader that arrived aboard the space station earlier this year.
The Commercially Enabled Rapid Space Science initiative experiment tests the device’s ability to detect and measure certain biomarkers such as antibodies, antigens, and proteins.
Use of the plate reader would allow scientists to analyze samples aboard the space station and obtain data quickly, rather than wait for the samples to return to Earth for analysis.

Ultimately, the research aims to support the timely detection of infections and other health issues in astronauts while expanding science capabilities in remote exploration locations where resupply will be more difficult.
A precision health investigation returns for its fourth and final planned stay aboard the space station to study how antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive and evolve in microgravity.
As part of the investigation, astronauts repeatedly sample surfaces throughout the space station to monitor for drug-resistant organisms.
The work could help develop ways to protect astronauts against bacterial infections during long-duration missions.
On Earth, the findings could provide insight into how superbugs develop from the overuse of antibiotics.

articles.title: NASA Demonstrates Next-Generation Heat Shield Technologies
paras: NASA is testing heat shields that can keep astronauts safe as they return from missions to the Moon and Mars in an unusual way: by taking out the trash.

When Northrop Grumman 24 th cargo resupply mission for NASA undocked from the International Space Station, it carried a fleet of 12 small, experimental capsules designed to test the next generation of thermal protection materials that could serve as the foundation for future heat shields.

The experiment, called the Kentucky Reentry Probe Experiment (KREPE-3), is the third in a series of low-cost, high-impact missions that use the final moments of the cargo spacecraft’s lifespan to gather valuable data.

The experiment is a collaboration among the University of Kentucky, the state of Kentucky, NASA’s Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR), several NASA centers, and other federal and commercial partners.
“KREPE-3 is a great example of the goals of NASA’s EPSCoR program,” said David Berger, EPSCoR program manager at NASA’s Headquarters in Washington.
“We are supporting the next generation of scientists and engineers as they develop unique projects that benefit their education and NASA’s mission goals.”
Before the mission’s Cygnus XL spacecraft departed the station, astronauts packed it with waste and activated the 12 small capsules carried inside.
Designed by University of Kentucky students, the capsules include sensors that will measure temperature, pressure, motion, magnetic field, and light during re-entry.
As the vehicle harmlessly breaks apart in Earth’s atmosphere on its planned route, the capsules will eject and begin collecting data on how each set of experimental heat shield materials performs.
Satellite signals will transfer live data to researchers, offering insights into how larger heat shields could protect future cargo or crew.
“It’s a smart way to get flight data on materials that are still in development,” said Keith Peterson, a materials engineer at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley.
“We’re essentially hitching a ride on a vehicle that’s already coming back to Earth.”
The capsules will carry a variety of thermal protective components, including proven technology such as the ceramic tile material used on the space shuttle.
Others will test new options, such as a 3D-printed heat shield from the Additive Manufacturing of Thermal Protective Systems project developed at NASA Johnson and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

Researchers at NASA Ames are contributing several materials to KREPE-3, including two capsules that will fly a next-generation family of protective coverings known as Materials Engineered for Re-entry using Innovative Needling Operations (MERINO).

Made from layers of carbon and phenolic fibers stitched together like felt, the materials are more flexible, faster to produce, and less expensive than traditional protective substances – making them promising candidates for Mars missions.
Thanks to Mars’ thinner atmosphere, missions to land on the Red Planet involve lower heat loads and allow for lighter protection.
A third capsule will combine those protective coverings with other elements.
The Kentucky Instrumented Conical Hypersonic Experiment will utilize a dual-cone shape.
It combines a tungsten tip attached to a cone layered with carbon and hear-resistant plastic fibers, and an aft cone wrapped in MERINO.
This unique design will validate computer models against real-world data.
Another capsule is shaped like the protective aeroshell that will protect NASA’s upcoming mission, Dragonfly, as it arrives at Saturn’s moon, Titan, and will test the dynamic stability of the design.

It is covered in Phenolic Impregnated Carbon Ablator, a material developed at NASA Ames that has applications for commercial vehicles and flew on NASA’s Stardust , Mars Science Laboratory , and Mars 2020 missions.
One capsule will test a deployable heat shield called Adaptable Deployable Entry and Placement Technology, which is shaped like an umbrella to increase surface area and slow descent.
At full scale, Adaptable Deployable Entry design could be folded, making it ideal for deploying payloads that are larger than the rockets that launch them into flight.

While some capsules are testing new materials to carry missions to Mars, others are testing new shapes and designs that will further research and understanding of computer modeling and sensor design — technologies that could open doors to another generation of re-entry design innovation.

Additional capsules developed by domestic and international partners will test a variety of known and new materials, including a heat flux sensor developed at the University of Stuttgart in Germany, that will help researchers measure how heat moves across a surface during re-entry.
“We’re pushing the boundaries of what heat shields can do,” said Peterson.
“And we’re testing them in a way that’s fast, affordable, and incredibly effective.”

articles.title: Floodwaters Overwhelm Thailand
paras: September falls in the heart of the monsoon season in Thailand, where cities and towns are accustomed to the afternoon rains and thunderstorms that frequently roll through.
But throughout late September and early October 2026, persistent heavy rains punctuated by intense downpours left low-lying areas across the country in Southeast Asia under sustained flooding.
Prachin Buri province was among the areas where flooding was widespread.
The right image above shows land along the Bang Pakong River and nearby agricultural areas and aquaculture facilities inundated on October 2, 2026.
The left image shows the same area at the same time of year in 2025.
Acquired with NASA-USGS Landsat satellites, the images are false-color to better distinguish water from vegetation, developed land, and other surfaces.
The bright red shapes are floating solar arrays.
Some of the flooding likely stemmed from a low-pressure system that stalled over the area for several days in late September.
Stoked by moisture and energy from the warm Gulf of Thailand nearby, the system delivered especially intense rains to the region.

About 100 kilometers (60 miles) to the west, Bangkok received nearly 300 millimeters (11.8 inches) of rain over a 48-hour period, according to news reports, close to the average monthly rainfall total for September of 344 millimeters (13.5 inches).

Since mid-September, flooding has occurred in 50 provinces across the country, affecting over 4 million people and causing dozens of deaths, according to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies .
Government agencies estimate about 270,000 hectares (670,000 acres) of farmland, including rice fields and fruit orchards, have been damaged.

articles.title: NASA Seeks US Industry Plans for Commercial Space Stations
paras: NASA is advancing American leadership in space by taking the next step toward a future where commercial space stations lead the way in low Earth orbit.
On Friday, the agency released its final Request for Proposals inviting industry to submit plans for the next generation of commercial space stations.

“In alignment with the President’s National Space Policy, NASA is committed to maintaining a sustained American presence in low Earth orbit long after the International Space Station retires,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.
“We will continue to need a place to conduct research, develop technologies, train crews, and prepare for missions to the Moon and Mars.

Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.”
Building on the agency’s Ignition event earlier this year, NASA regularly has engaged with private industry to shape the agency’s future direction in low Earth orbit.
This included publishing two Requests for Information in March to gather industry’s perspective on low Earth orbit destinations and transportation.

The agency also published a draft Request for Proposals in July, followed by an industry day and one-on-one meetings that allowed interested companies to review and comment on the planned acquisition approach.
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” said Isaacman.
“Since Ignition, we have spent a lot of time listening to industry and working through what it will take to make this transition successful.
The opportunity is significant, but the economics ultimately have to work.
We want to see credible plans, strong technical execution, and companies prepared to invest in destinations that can serve NASA while developing additional customers and markets of their own.”
Proposals are due Tuesday, Dec. 8, with contract awards expected in spring 2027.

Under the solicitation, NASA outlines requirements for companies interested in designing, building, testing, certifying, and operating commercial low Earth orbit destinations capable of providing end-to-end destination and transportation services for human spaceflight use.

NASA intends to award firm-fixed-price, multi-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contracts supporting development, certification, and services for continued low Earth orbit research and exploration.

This will allow NASA to select two or more contractors through early development, followed by a competitive task order for final design, test, and evaluation, as well as certification and services from one or more contractors.

articles.title: NASA’s SSPICY Mission to Demonstrate In-Space Inspection Technologies
paras: A new NASA-supported spacecraft will get up close to satellites that are no longer in service, demonstrating technologies that could support future in-space repairs and reduce orbital debris.
The Small Spacecraft Propulsion and Inspection Capability (SSPICY) mission launched Oct. 1 from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California.
The mission is a technology demonstration where an Otter spacecraft will approach up to four inoperable space objects of U.S. origin in low Earth orbit, such as satellites and rocket bodies.

In early 2027, the Otter spacecraft, built by Starfish Space, will begin to navigate within hundreds of yards of each object to perform inspections, using autonomous guidance and control software with minimal input from ground controllers.
Computer vision and sensors enable software to make real-time navigation decisions as the spacecraft approaches each target.
During inspection, the Otter spacecraft will gather critical information about each object, such as spin rate, orientation, and surface condition.

An electric propulsion system will enable SSPICY to travel between objects, and an articulating robotic boom will test pointing the spacecraft’s thrusters for precise maneuvering between different orbits.
This mission is the first time these technologies will be tested together as an integrated system, paving the way for future autonomous servicing and orbital debris inspection.

During the SSPICY mission, the Otter spacecraft won’t touch or dock with any satellites, but will test the technologies needed to one day enable missions to service or repair objects in orbit, or to safely remove them by pulling them into Earth’s atmosphere for disposal.

Space objects like rocket bodies and satellites that are experiencing issues or no longer in service can break apart or collide with one another, creating varying forms of orbital debris from large fragments to small particles.

With thousands of satellites launched each year to provide communications, weather forecasting, navigation, and other services that people rely on daily, keeping the space near Earth safe for operations is increasingly critical.
Starfish Space developed and operates the Otter 24C spacecraft, which is performing the SSPICY mission.
NASA’s Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program within the agency’s Research and Technology Mission Directorate funds and manages the technology demonstration.

NASA’s Small Business Innovation Research / Small Business Technology Transfer program funded awards to Starfish Space to support early development of the spacecraft’s key technologies and capabilities.

articles.title: NASA Briefing to Highlight Contributions to Martian Moons Mission
paras: Media are invited to join NASA for a media teleconference at 4 p.m. EDT, Thursday, Oct. 15, to preview the agency’s contributions to JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission.
The mission is scheduled to launch from JAXA’s Tanegashima Space Center in Japan on Monday, Oct. 19 EDT (Tuesday, Oct. 20 JST).
Audio of the media teleconference will stream on the agency’s website at:

The MMX spacecraft will arrive at Mars in August 2027 to begin its survey of the Red Planet’s two moons, Phobos and Deimos.
After surveying Phobos in detail, the spacecraft will collect a sample of the moon’s surface no earlier than December 2028 and deliver it to Earth in 2031.

NASA’s contributions to the mission include the MEGANE gamma-ray and neutron spectrometer, the spacecraft’s surface sampler mechanism, and communications and navigation support from the agency’s Deep Space Network , as well as funding United States scientists participating on the MMX science team.
The MEGANE instrument was developed by Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory.
Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, developed the spacecraft’s pneumatic sampler mechanism.
NASA’s contributions to the MMX mission were funded by the agency’s Discovery Program, which provides frequent flight opportunities for high-value, focused planetary science investigations.

articles.title: NASA Sets Coverage for SpaceX 35th Station Resupply Launch, Arrival
paras: NASA and SpaceX are targeting 6:33 a.m. EDT, Tuesday, Oct. 13, for the next launch to deliver science investigations, supplies, and equipment, including the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, to the space station.

articles.title: NASA’s Curiosity Looks Back After Reaching Elevation Milestone

articles.title: NASA’s SpaceX 35th Commercial Resupply Mission Overview
paras: NASA and SpaceX are targeting no earlier than Tuesday, Oct. 13 to launch scientific investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.

Loaded with more than 6,300 pounds of supplies, the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft will lift off aboard the company’s Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.
Following its arrival to the orbital complex, Dragon will autonomously dock to the space-facing port of the space station’s Harmony module.
NASA will stream launch and docking coverage through a variety of platforms.
Learn where to watch online:
For more than 25 years, the International Space Station has supported research by scientists from more than 110 countries, enabling more than 4,000 experiments in microgravity.
Research conducted aboard the station helps advance long-duration missions to the Moon as part of the Artemis program and to Mars, while also providing multiple benefits to humanity.
In addition to cargo for the crew aboard the space station, Dragon will deliver several new science experiments, including:
With LambdaVision-1 , NASA is testing how to manufacture artificial eye retinas in microgravity, building them one thin layer at a time.
Reduced settling in microgravity may create more uniform, stable layers, potentially improving implants’ performance.
These artificial retinas could help restore vision for patients with currently incurable retinal diseases on Earth.
NASA will use the Stellar Spheroids experiment to study how microgravity affects the growth and function of 3D human heart tissue models.
Researchers will assess whether microgravity improves the formation of advanced vascular networks.
Results could help researchers develop more realistic heart tissue models for disease research and support larger‑scale drug testing on future space missions.
Using non-traditional elements, ELF-Unconventional Glass 2 studies how glass forms in microgravity.
Researchers will observe molten behavior in space, then return solid samples to Earth for detailed analysis.
These unconventional glasses could offer higher strength, improved optical capabilities, and greater durability for spacecraft, habitats, and other exploration technologies.
The MINDS experiment studies brain organoids to better understand inflammation linked to neurodegenerative diseases.
The investigation uses “organoid villages,” which combine cells from multiple people to better represent patient diversity.
Results could help identify new treatment targets for diseases like Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and multiple sclerosis.
NASA astronauts Anil Menon and Jessica Watkins will monitor the Dragon spacecraft’s arrival.
It will remain docked to the orbiting laboratory for about a month before splashing down in the Pacific Ocean, returning critical science and hardware to teams on Earth.

International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays (IROSA) – The final pair of IROSAs that will be installed on the space station, completing the augmentation of its power system to support critical operations, including its safe and controlled deorbit.
Collapsible Continency Urinal and supporting hardware – A demonstration and test unit supporting NASA’s Artemis III mission.
Canadarm2 joint flight support equipment – A large foam clamshell will fly empty to return the failed robotic arm joint that was replaced during a June 30 spacewalk.
After its return to Earth, teams will analyze the joint on the ground.

Additional equipment launching includes a toilet dose pump, a toilet pretreat quality sensor, and a robot micro-conical tool used for space station maintenance and utilization tasks with external replacement units and payloads.

When Dragon returns in mid‑November, it will bring back the failed joint on the Canadarm2 for analysis and refurbishment, a spacesuit for ground refurbishment, a fluid- and pressure-control pump assembly from the urine processor, and a filtration unit for the water processor assembly.

articles.title: A Journey to the Depths of Ancient Mars?
paras: News and Features Multimedia Mars Missions Mars Home Written by Alex Jones, Ph.D. candidate at Imperial College London

After spending the last six months exploring “ Lac de Charmes ,” a region of ancient rock beyond Jezero crater’s western rim, Perseverance has stumbled upon a vast field of light-toned rocks peppering the Martian surface.
Light-colored rocks are a strange sight on Mars , a planet dominated by dark-colored basaltic rocks.
This many light-colored rocks in one place piqued the Science Team’s interest… what are they?
How did they get here?
To answer the first question, Perseverance has been investigating the composition and textures of these rocks.
Data so far indicates that many of them are igneous rocks called gabbro, which are dominated by minerals rich in iron and magnesium.
Such rocks typically form by slow cooling and crystallization of magma deep in the crust.
So how did these deep fragments of Mars find their way to the surface?
Perseverance has spent the last week trying to answer this question by investigating a patch of possible bedrock poking out between the light-toned boulders and loose regolith.
Initial images suggest that the rock is made up of light- and dark-colored, angular fragments of rock, forming what geologists call a breccia.
One possibility the team is investigating is that the light-toned boulders scattered across the hillside have eroded out of this breccia.
Breccias often form through violent processes involving the fracturing and transport of rock to produce their angular shapes.
Layers of breccia observed outside Jezero have previously been attributed to asteroid impacts on early Mars .
Perhaps similar impacts (or the Jezero impact itself?) could be responsible for digging up these light-colored blocks.
Only time (and of course, Perseverance), will tell.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5029-5035: Back in the Lab
paras: News and Features Multimedia Mars Missions Mars Home 2 min read
Written by Michelle Minitti, MAHLI Deputy Principal Investigator
The majority of Curiosity plans involve mosaics from Mastcam and ChemCam, chemistry analyses from ChemCam and APXS, images from MAHLI and MARDI, and systematic measurements from REMS, RAD, and DAN.
It is only when we stop to drill that we fully live up to our Mars Science Laboratory designation, using CheMin and SAM to analyze Martian rock.

This was one such week, where our focus was wrapping up CheMin analysis of a sample from the “Basque Lakes” drill hole (pictured above), preparing SAM for its analysis, and analyzing the sample with the SAM tunable laser spectrometer (TLS).

The CheMin data were key to SAM deciding to analyze the sample at all, and SAM will wait to receive the results from the TLS run (measurement of the volatiles present) to decide if they want to follow up with a separate mass spectrometry analysis next week.

The laboratory activities require a significant portion of the daily power budget of the rover so the rest of the payload largely takes a back seat during drill campaigns, a worthy trade for CheMin and SAM’s valuable data.
However, using the power that was available, we gathered data to contextualize our drill location and continued our systematic environmental monitoring.
Mastcam acquired a 360-degree mosaic of our surroundings to build a full picture of the geologic setting of the sample.

Its color and improved resolution relative to Navcam also guided subsequent science requests, such as more focused Mastcam imaging of structures near the workspace, and ChemCam RMI imaging of the “Cordillera” butte.
Mastcam, coupled with Navcam, also planned a series of seven photometry observations spread across fixed times of day.
These observations evaluate how the observed spectral characteristics of targets change as the Sun angle on them changes.
They help us better interpret images from the rover and from cameras in orbit.

ChemCam gathered more chemistry data from the variety of materials in the workspace, from the Basque Lakes drill hole interior, to sand ripples (“French Creek”) covering the bedrock, to loose gray clasts of unknown origin (“Wooley” and “Fireside”) sprinkled across the workspace.
Our environmental monitoring activities included regular REMS, RAD, and DAN measurements and Navcam and Mastcam monitoring of dust loading in the atmosphere, cloud activity, and dust-devil activity.

articles.title: Lunar Grounding Challenge
paras: As an astronaut traverses the lunar South Pole, tribocharging from walking on the lunar surface and plasma charging from the ambient plasma generate electric charge on the spacesuit.
This problem is severely compounded when entering lunar shadows and Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs).
In these dark zones, the spacesuit can buildup a substantial negative potential due to a lack of ambient ion flux and the absence of photoelectron emission to balance ambient electron collection.
The risk occurs when an astronaut returns to the spacecraft.
Because the lunar surface lacks a natural environmental mechanism to bleed the charge accumulated on spacesuit away, the astronaut may become a walking, high voltage capacitor.
In the sunlit region, the stationary lander will hold slightly positive electrical potential.

When a highly negatively-charged astronaut approaches the vehicle, the extreme voltage differential can trigger electrostatic discharge (an instantaneous electrical arc, or a spark) during physical contact.

A rapid discharge from the astronaut to the lander risks degrading vital suit layers, damaging sensitive suit electronics, threatening the oxygen-rich environment inside the suit, and delivering dangerous electrical shocks to the crew.

Through the Lunar Grounding Challenge, NASA is seeking innovative designs and operational solutions to provide a lunar bringing to equilibrium capability to safely discharge a suited astronaut from high triboelectric charge buildup during lunar surface EVAs in the South Pole.

This challenge seeks innovative concepts for an Electrostatic Discharge (ESD) mitigation solution to neutralize the astronaut in a safe and timely manner under this extreme charge differential before astronauts directly interact with the lander.

articles.title: Curiosity Blog, Sols 5022-5028: Cashing in at Cache Creek
paras: News and Features Multimedia Mars Missions Mars Home 3 min read
Written by Lucy Thompson, Senior Research Scientist, University of New Brunswick, Canada
Before we landed, the area of Gale crater that we planned to explore was divided up into rectangular parcels with designated names.
The names were chosen after small towns associated with significant geological features.
Our selected targets (mesas, bedrock, soil, boulders, etc.) within those quads were then given unofficial names based on the theme of the quad.
See the link here for more details on naming conventions on Mars.

Curiosity has long since climbed above the quads that were selected before landing, and before her 14-year, 38-kilometer (24.6-mile) trek, which included more than 1 kilometer (0.6 miles) of elevation gain.
We recently entered the new Cache Creek quad, named after an area of geological diversity in British Columbia, Canada.

The area in Canada includes exposures of oceanic crust, marine sediments, volcanic rocks, and glacial deposits, as well as being home to lakes with unusual chemistry that may be analogous to lakes that once existed on Mars.
It also lies at the southern end of the 1860s Gold Rush Trail, where miners and prospectors flocked to this part of British Columbia in search of riches.
This week we successfully drilled into our 48th rock target in Gale crater (“Basque Lakes”), from the Cache Creek quad.
While we may not literally strike gold, we are all eagerly anticipating the outcome of the CheMin X-ray diffraction analysis of our drilled sample that will take place in this weekend plan.
What gold mine of minerals will the sample contain?

What can they tell us about the depositional and alteration history of this rock exposure — might there be similar minerals present as those associated with some of the lakes in the Cache Creek area of British Columbia?
As an APXS uplink lead and strategic planner this week I helped to plan the triage contact science on the potential Basque Lakes drill target and communicate the results to the rest of the team.
We placed APXS in contact with the rock target to measure its chemistry, and the MAHLI camera to within 1 centimeter (about 0.4 inches) to examine in detail the textures .
ChemCam also fired its laser at the Basque Lakes drill target to further characterize composition.
MAHLI also imaged the target after the engineers checked the stability of the rock with a pre-load test .
The results from all these activities helped to determine whether to proceed with drilling.
Despite significant power constraints associated with drilling and the accompanying analyses, as well as an aging rover, we were also able to plan additional activities.
Mastcam imaged the surrounding terrain to provide context for our new drill sample.

ChemCam was able to analyze the chemistry of another nearby bedrock target, “Peace River,” and use its imaging and passive spectroscopic capabilities to look at the new drill hole and surrounding tailings.
ChemCam remote imaging was also used to examine an interesting-looking deposit of jumbled blocks at the base of a nearby butte, “Cordillera.”
We also utilized Navcam and Mastcam imaging in the continued monitoring of environmental and atmospheric conditions in Gale crater.

Analysis of the Basque Lakes drill sample should continue next week with delivery of material to SAM, which will reveal more nuggets of information regarding the history of this particular rock sample.
Curiosity will likely be at this location for another week, before we dump the sample and drive away to continue our exploration of Mount Sharp and Gale crater.

articles.title: Mapping the Gaps in NASA’s Return to the Moon, featuring Richard Spolzino
paras: “I want to be able to look at a rocket launch and say, ‘I touched a piece of this.’”
That’s how Richard Spolzino describes the thing he’s chasing.
Not a title, not a specific mission, not even NASA itself, just the ability to point at something real and know his work made it possible.

At NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia, Spolzino works within Moon Base’s mission architecture and systems interoperability effort, helping identify what NASA still doesn’t know about the Moon and Mars, and making sure that missing information gets found before it becomes a problem.
“ For me, it kept coming back to where can I have the most impact?
Where can my work touch the most things?
Spolzino didn’t set out to end up here.
He started college as a history major.
He switched to a physics track at Santa Clara University, thinking he’d end up in astrophysics.
A research stint at Lick Observatory studying interstellar dust polarization taught him two things: the work was fascinating and, “I don’t think the staying-up-all-night thing is for me,” he says.
After graduation, he started down the path of Officer Candidate School in the Navy, hoping to fly jets.

It didn’t pan out, and that detour led him to a graduate program at the University of Houston, combining aerospace engineering and space architecture — not the habitat-design kind of architecture people usually picture, but the systems-level kind, where a lunar oxygen plant connects to the rovers that feed it, which connect to the processor, which connects to the user drawing down the resource.
“I was always more attracted to how all the pieces work together than to any single piece,” he says.
Ask Spolzino if he dreamed of working at NASA, and the honest answer is no.
“I really admire people who’ve had that drive their whole life,” he says.
“For me, it kept coming back to where can I have the most impact?
Where can my work touch the most things?”
A University of Houston program with strong ties to Johnson Space Center put NASA on his radar alongside other options in industry and government.
What ultimately drew him in wasn’t the agency’s name, it was the scope of the problems and the direct line he saw to senior decision-makers shaping the return to the Moon.
That’s also, he adds, exactly why NASA is worth considering for people who aren’t sure it’s their calling yet.

The culture rewards people willing to take on more than their assigned lane and gives early-career employees room to grow into problems bigger than their job description, something he says he might not have found moving up more slowly in industry.
Spolzino’s day-to-day work centers on a deceptively simple idea: the data gap.
“You can think of it as synonymous with a knowledge gap,” he explains.
“It’s a way of documenting the thing we don’t know.”
Take the geotechnical properties of lunar regolith — moon dust, essentially, but the specifics matter enormously.
How much weight can it bear?
What’s its shear strength?
Answering those questions shapes everything from how far a rover can safely drive to whether a habitat’s foundation will hold.

A data gap lays that out formally: what we don’t know, why it matters, what we currently have that falls short, and, critically, a specific measurable target industry and international partners can aim for.
“Once we’ve identified what’s missing,” he says, “our partners can look at that list and see exactly where their contribution would be valuable.”
His team started with roughly 25 published data gaps last year.
They’re on track for 60 by the end of this year.
The concept only matters if it changes decisions, and Spolzino cites two recent examples where it did.

When the lunar lander company now known as Voyager (formerly Astrobotic) was preparing its upcoming Griffin-1 mission, the team didn’t help them figure out what instruments to fly since that was already locked in.
Instead, Spolzino’s team helped them prioritize what data gets sent home first through a communication pipeline that can’t carry everything at once.
“How do you prioritize all the things you say you want, and what gets sent back through that constrained pipeline?” he asks.

On the other side of the pipeline, Spolzino has spent recent months evaluating proposed instruments (spectrometers, sample collection tools, tech demonstrations) against the published data gaps to help leadership decide what’s worth flying.
Some proposals map cleanly onto a documented need.
Others don’t align with anything NASA has said it’s missing.
“That’s used to filter down what gets pushed forward as a real candidate,” he says.
Industry partners have taken notice, and leadership now asks companies pitching new instruments to show how their proposal maps to a data gap before the conversation goes any further.

Spolzino admits the job reshaped an assumption he carried out of graduate school — that NASA had everything figured out, and that the agency’s reputation meant every question already had an answer somewhere inside its walls.
Three years in, he sees it differently.
“Keeping the kind of reputation NASA has takes constant, deliberate work,” he says.
“Everyone’s genuinely trying to pull in the right direction, but it’s not automatic.”
That realization was clarifying for him.
The agency runs on people figuring things out in real time, which means there’s room for someone early in their career to contribute meaningfully, rather than just executing someone else’s playbook.
His advice to students considering NASA is practical, not sentimental: Grades matter less than people think.
“The projects you work on, and the results of that work, are what people look at first,” he says.
His advice is to join clubs, take on real projects, and build something.
“It’s less about credentials and more about giving yourself something to show up with.”
Spolzino was already deep into the second book, The Dark Forest , on a flight from New York to Houston when the plane was diverted to San Antonio.
“I did not care that I was three or four hours late,” he says.
“I had that book, and I was just devouring it.”
An older game, but a formative one.
Spolzino credits it with cementing his interest in space before college even started.

“It’s a space program simulator where you build rockets piece by piece, and the physics are simplified but accurate enough that you’re doing a lot of the same math as an actual mission design tool,” he says.
“That really had a huge impact on me figuring out that space was the thing I wanted to do.”

articles.title: Rains Swamp the Gandak River
paras: Storms drenched Nepal’s mountainous Lumbini and Gandaki provinces with waves of torrential rain between September 24 and 27 .
The deluge, arriving late in the monsoon season, triggered landslides and pushed the Gandak River, also called the Narayani, to record levels in both Nepal and India.
With runoff streaming into the braided river system , water overtopped and breached embankments in several areas, inundating farmland and settlements along the river for hundreds of kilometers.
As authorities assessed the full extent of the damage, news reports indicated that flooding and landslides had affected hundreds of villages and displaced thousands of people.

Images captured by MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra and Aqua satellites on September 20, 2026 (left), and September 29, 2026 (right), show the extent of the flooding.
The false-color images combine observations of infrared and visible light (MODIS bands 7-2-1 ) to make it easier to distinguish the water.
Floodwater appears blue; vegetation is bright green; clouds are light blue.
In many areas, water inundated seasonal fields on low-lying deposits of sand and silt within the river’s channel, called diara , where flooding is expected.
However, it also breached embankments and flooded several settled areas, including parts of Bagaha , Areraj , and Fulia Khand .
Data from Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology indicated that a gauge in Devghāṭ reached as high as 11.94 meters on September 27, the highest since measurements began there in the 1960s.
According to news reports , gauges in India along the Gandak that set new high-water marks included Bagaha, Dumariaghat, Rewaghat, and Lalganj.
NASA has several tools and datasets available for tracking rainfall and flooding.
Among them are Worldview , FLOOD Viewer , and the GPM IMERG Global Viewer .
